stages.title: Plate tectonics
stages.hook: The east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa look like jigsaw pieces. Is that a coincidence?
explain: Earth's rigid outer shell (the lithosphere) is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. They move slowly, a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow, carried by slow movement in the hot mantle below.

Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 using matching coastlines, fossils and rocks on different continents. Many scientists rejected it because he could not explain what pushed the continents. In the 1950s and 1960s, studies of the sea floor, including spreading at mid-ocean ridges and magnetic stripes, led to the theory of plate tectonics.

At divergent boundaries plates move apart and new crust forms, like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. At convergent boundaries plates collide: one may sink under the other (subduction), or two continents crumple to form mountains, as the Himalayas formed when India met Asia. At transform boundaries plates slide past each other, as along the San Andreas Fault.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries. The Pacific "Ring of Fire" is the best-known belt.

example.q: The Atlantic floor spreads at about 2.5 cm a year on each side, so the two sides move apart at 5 cm a year. How far apart do they move in 20 million years?
steps: Rate: 5 cm per year = 0.05 m per year.

stages.title: Volcanoes and earthquakes
stages.hook: Why do volcanoes and earthquakes cluster in the same belts around the world?
explain: A volcano is an opening in the crust where magma (molten rock) reaches the surface as lava, ash and gas. Most are near subduction zones and ridges, but a few, like Hawaii, sit over hot spots in the mantle.

Shield volcanoes have gentle slopes and runny lava. Composite (strato) volcanoes are steep and can erupt explosively. Not all eruptions are alike: gas content and the thickness (viscosity) of magma matter.

An earthquake is shaking caused by sudden release of stress along a fault. The point underground where it starts is the focus. The point on the surface directly above is the epicentre. Seismometers record the waves.

Magnitude measures energy released. Each step up on the moment magnitude scale means the shaking amplitude is ten times bigger and the energy about 32 times bigger. Earthquakes under the sea can cause tsunamis.

stages.title: Rivers and landscape formation
stages.hook: How can a gentle river carve a canyon as deep as the Grand Canyon?
explain: Rivers shape land by erosion (wearing away), transport (carrying material) and deposition (dropping it). Their power depends on how fast the water moves and how much rock and sand it carries.

Near the source, the river is steep and fast and cuts down, making narrow V-shaped valleys with rapids and waterfalls. In the middle course it widens. In the lower course, where the land is flat, it swings in bends called meanders.

Over time the outside of a bend erodes and the inside builds up. A meander can get cut off, leaving an oxbow lake. After floods, rivers drop sediment on the floodplain, making fertile soil. Where a river reaches the sea and slows, it may build a delta, like the Nile or Mississippi delta.
Waterfalls form where a river crosses a band of hard rock lying over softer rock; the soft rock wears away faster, leaving a drop.

stages.title: Ocean currents and tides
stages.hook: The sea rises and falls twice a day on many coasts. What pulls the ocean?
explain: Ocean currents are large streams of water moving through the ocean. Surface currents are pushed by winds and bent by Earth's spin (the Coriolis effect), forming huge loops called gyres: clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern.

Warm currents carry heat away from the tropics. The Gulf Stream and its extension help keep north-west Europe milder than other places at the same latitude. Cold currents such as the Humboldt (Peru) Current bring cold water along the west coast of South America and support rich fisheries.
Deep currents are driven by differences in temperature and salt, and make up a slow global "conveyor belt" that takes hundreds to a thousand years to circulate.

Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity, with help from the Sun. Most coasts have two high and two low tides each day, about 12 hours 25 minutes apart. Spring tides (biggest range) happen at new and full Moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up. Neap tides (smallest range) happen at the quarter Moons.

example.q: High tide occurs at 06:00. About when is the next high tide?
steps: High tides are about 12 h 25 min apart.

stages.title: Atmospheric circulation
stages.hook: Why do ships and planes use certain routes, and why do deserts line up at similar latitudes?
explain: The Sun heats the equator most. Warm air rises there, creating low pressure and heavy rain. The air spreads out, cools and sinks around 30° N and 30° S, where it makes high pressure and dry weather, which is why many deserts (Sahara, Arabian, Kalahari, Australian) lie near these latitudes.

Surface air flows from high to low pressure. Earth's spin bends winds (Coriolis effect), creating the trade winds (blowing toward the equator from the east), the westerlies (mid-latitudes, from the west) and the polar easterlies.

These loops form three circulation cells in each hemisphere: the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells. The meeting zone near the equator is the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), which moves north and south with the seasons and brings monsoon rains to places like India and West Africa.
Local winds also matter. In the day, land heats faster than sea, so a sea breeze blows toward the land. At night the breeze reverses.

stages.title: Ecosystems and biomes
stages.hook: A rainforest and a desert both have living things. Why are the plants and animals so different?
explain: An ecosystem is a community of living things and their non-living surroundings, linked by energy and nutrients. A biome is a very large region with a similar climate and similar vegetation. Examples are tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, temperate forest, grassland, taiga and tundra.

Producers (plants and algae) make food from sunlight. Consumers eat other living things: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals. Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.
Energy passes along food chains, and most of it is lost as heat at each step, so there are fewer top predators than plants. Many food chains link together in a food web.

Living things are adapted to their biome. Cacti store water and have spines. Polar bears have thick fur and fat. Rainforest trees grow tall to reach sunlight. Biodiversity, the variety of life, is highest in tropical rainforests and coral reefs.

example.q: In a food chain, grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, which is the producer and which is the top consumer?
steps: Grass makes food by photosynthesis, so it is the producer.

So the snake is the top consumer.

stages.title: Population distribution and migration
stages.hook: Why do some people leave their homes for far-off places while others stay for life?
explain: Population is not spread evenly. Densely populated regions include South Asia, East Asia, Western Europe and the Nile valley. Sparsely populated ones include deserts, polar lands, high mountains and tropical rainforests.

Population change depends on births, deaths and migration. Natural increase = birth rate − death rate (per 1,000 people). The demographic transition model describes how birth and death rates change as countries develop: death rates fall first, so population grows quickly; later birth rates fall too.

Migration is moving to live in a new place. Push factors drive people away, such as war, drought, poverty or lack of jobs. Pull factors attract them, such as work, safety, schools or family. Internal migration is within a country; international migration crosses borders. Refugees flee danger or persecution.
Migration has existed throughout human history. It changes both the places people leave and the places they arrive: remittances support families, and migrants add skills, culture and labour.

stages.title: Agriculture and industrial geography
stages.hook: Why is rice grown in flooded fields in Asia but wheat on dry plains in Canada and Ukraine?
explain: Farming depends on climate, soil, relief (the shape of land) and markets. Subsistence farming grows food mainly for the farmer's family. Commercial farming grows food to sell. Intensive farming gets a large output from a small area using lots of labour or inputs; extensive farming uses large areas with less input per hectare.

Rice needs warm temperatures and plenty of water, so it suits monsoon Asia. Wheat prefers cooler, drier temperate plains. Cocoa grows only in hot, wet lands near the equator, mainly in West Africa, South America and Southeast Asia. Pastoral farmers in dry lands herd animals such as camels, cattle and sheep.

Industry is grouped into sectors. The primary sector takes raw materials (farming, mining, fishing). The secondary sector manufactures goods. The tertiary sector provides services such as teaching, shops and transport. The quaternary sector deals with information and research. As countries develop, more workers shift from primary toward tertiary jobs.

Industries locate where costs are lowest: near raw materials, energy, workers, markets or ports. The Industrial Revolution began in Britain around 1760, with coal and iron nearby. Today much manufacturing is in East Asia and many services are global.

example.q: A country has 100 workers: 10 primary, 30 secondary, 60 tertiary. What percentage is in services?
steps: Services are the tertiary sector: 60 workers.

stages.title: Urban geography
stages.hook: In 1950 only a few cities had 10 million people. Today there are dozens. How do cities grow and what problems follow?
explain: Urbanisation is the increasing share of people living in towns and cities. Since about 2007, more than half of the world's people live in cities. Cities grow by natural increase and by migration from the countryside (rural-to-urban migration).
A megacity has more than 10 million people. Examples include Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, São Paulo, Cairo, Lagos and Mexico City. Most of today's fastest growth is in Asia and Africa.

Inside a city, land uses are arranged in zones. The central business district (CBD) has the highest land values, tall buildings, offices and shops. Residential areas surround it, and factories often sit near transport links. Land is cheaper at the edges, so cities spread outward in urban sprawl.

Rapid growth brings challenges: housing shortages and informal settlements, traffic, pollution, and pressure on water and sanitation. Good planning provides public transport, green spaces and affordable homes.

example.q: A city had 8 million people and grew to 12 million. By what percentage did it grow?

analogies.home: A crowded bus makes you stand close together; cities have the same problem with space.
analogies.city: Metro trains move many people using little street space.
